newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia under fire for leading live animal trade.
newsitem.headline: Australia under fire for leading live animal trade.

text.p: The billion dollar world trade in live animal exports has come under renewed attack after the drowning of 1,600 Australian cattle off Guam at the weekend.
Animal welfare campaigners are shifting the focus of their protests from Europe to Australia as a result of the sinking of the Philippine-registered Guernsey Express by Typhoon Dale.

It is the second disaster to hit Australia's flourishing live export trade in two months. In September, almost 70,000 Australian sheep perished when the Panamanian-registered Uniceb caught fire and sank off the Seychelles.
"Australia is bloody unlucky," commented Lloyd Beeby, head of international sheepmeat and livestock marketing at the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC).
The 300-kph (185-mph) winds and 15-metre seas whipped up by Typhoon Dale were totally outside AMLC's control, he said.
Beeby said three sinkings of ships transporting Australian live animals since 1980 had come despite stringent safety standards.
But animal welfare groups rejected the AMLC's defence.

Australia's Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA) has allocated funds for a major advertising campaign to bring exports to a stop, although it is first giving the national government a chance to tighten up the rules, RSPCA national president Hugh Wirth said.

Eric Ball, RSPCA Western Australian state president, said the organisation objected to codes of practice, ventilation standards and a lack of veterinarians and Australian stockmen on board ship to look after the animals.
"They're purely practical things and are not being addressed at all. It's just being allowed to drift along," he said.
The Sydney-based Animal Liberation group said it was working with the London-based International Fund for Animal Welfare and Compassion in World Farming to end live animal exports.
"I want to end the live cattle trade and the live sheep trade -- enough is enough," said Richard Jones, a member of the New South Wales state parliament and Animal Liberation.
Experts say the trade is now worth as much as US$1 billion, with Australia's share jumping to A$523 million ($413 million) in 1995/96 from A$182 million in 1992/93.
Traditionally the world's largest sheep exporter, Australia has recently overtaken Ireland as live cattle export leader too.

In 1995/96 Australia exported 5.5 million live sheep, worth more than A$207 million, mainly to the Middle East. Exports of live cattle in the same year amounted to more than 627,000 head worth more than A$316 million, mainly bound for Indonesia and the Philippines but also, in smaller quantities, for Japan.

Having risen largely in response to the high cost of slaughter in Australia, the live animal trade has begun to generate increasingly ambitious calls from within the industry for innovations such as "slaughter on the water".

New Zealand, which about two years ago lifted export bans, follows Australia as second-largest live sheep exporter in the world. But it conducts its trade in a much better regulated and more humane way than Australia, an RSPCA spokeswoman said.

Ireland is the second-biggest live cattle exporter and Britain is also a major exporter. About 1.2 million sheep and 500,000 veal calves left Britain in 1994, prompting sometimes violent protests by animal rights activists blocking ports.

The United States also exported cattle to the Philippines while live cattle trade flowed both ways between the U.S. and Mexico.The only reason for Argentina's absence from the live cattle trade has been foot and mouth disease.
